clinicalPearls: Consider in any patient with chronic diarrhoea, bloating, weight loss, or unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia, even without overt GI symptoms
Can present atypically with isolated osteoporosis, infertility, elevated transaminases, peripheral neuropathy, or dental enamel defects
Dermatitis herpetiformis is a specific cutaneous marker and is essentially pathognomonic when biopsy-confirmed
Serologic testing must be performed while the patient is still on a gluten-containing diet, otherwise antibody titres normalise and results are falsely negative
First-degree relatives and patients with type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease, or Down/Turner syndrome have markedly increased prevalence and warrant screening
Selective IgA deficiency can cause false-negative IgA-based serology, so total IgA should be checked concurrently
Symptomatic response to a gluten-free diet supports but does not confirm the diagnosis; histology and serology should ideally precede dietary change
harrison.pathophysiology: Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten (from wheat, barley, and rye) in genetically susceptible individuals, most of whom carry HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. Deamidation of gluten peptides by tissue transglutaminase enhances their binding to these HLA molecules, driving an aberrant T-cell response that damages small intestinal enterocytes. The resulting villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis impair mucosal absorptive surface area, leading to malabsorption of macronutrients and micronutrients.
additionalDifferentials: Crohn disease of the small bowel
additionalInvestigations: IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody — first-line serologic screen, high sensitivity and specificity
Total serum IgA — excludes IgA deficiency causing false-negative serology
IgA or IgG deamidated gliadin peptide antibody — useful adjunct, especially in young children or IgA-deficient patients
Upper endoscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies — confirms diagnosis via villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis
HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping — high negative predictive value, useful to exclude disease when serology/histology are equivocal
Complete blood count and iron studies — screens for iron-deficiency anaemia from malabsorption
Bone mineral density (DEXA) — assesses for osteopenia/osteoporosis from calcium/vitamin D malabsorption
Fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E, K) and folate/B12 — evaluates extent of malabsorption
redFlags: Persistent or worsening symptoms despite strict gluten-free diet — consider refractory coeliac disease or alternative diagnosis
New abdominal pain, obstruction, or GI bleeding in a known coeliac patient — raises concern for enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma or ulcerative jejunoileitis
Severe malnutrition, hypoalbuminemia, or electrolyte derangement requiring urgent nutritional support
Unexplained weight loss with anaemia in an older adult — exclude malignancy alongside coeliac workup
Signs of adrenal or severe metabolic crisis from long-standing malabsorption
pitfalls: Testing serology after the patient has already started a gluten-free diet, producing false-negative results
Relying on serology alone without confirmatory duodenal biopsy, or biopsying too few sites reducing diagnostic yield
Missing the diagnosis in atypical presentations (isolated anaemia, infertility, elevated liver enzymes) because classic diarrhoea is absent
Failing to screen at-risk relatives or patients with associated autoimmune conditions
harrison.prognosis: Most patients respond well to strict, lifelong adherence to a gluten-free diet, with resolution of symptoms and mucosal healing over months to years. A small subset develops refractory disease or, rarely, enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma, particularly with prolonged undiagnosed or poorly controlled disease.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Celiac Disease (Gastroenterology section, Disorders of Malabsorption)
management: Strict lifelong gluten-free diet excluding wheat, barley and rye as the definitive treatment, supervised by a dietitian.
Correction of micronutrient deficiencies including iron, folate, vitamin B12, vitamin D and calcium.
Bone-health protection with dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and calcium and vitamin D supplementation as needed.
Pneumococcal vaccination in view of the functional hyposplenism associated with the disease.

Monitoring of dietary adherence and mucosal recovery, including tissue transglutaminase antibody trends, with investigation of non-response for refractory disease or enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma.
Screening of first-degree relatives and for associated autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes.
Dapsone alongside the gluten-free diet for coexisting dermatitis herpetiformis, with gastroenterology and dietetic multidisciplinary follow-up.
